subtopics.name: Key points
points: Momentum is a vector — always assign signs/directions before computing $\Delta p$.
Impulse and momentum share units (N·s = kg·m/s); impulse is the area under the force–time graph.
For a FIXED momentum change, force and time trade off: $F_{avg} = \Delta p/\Delta t$.
$F = dp/dt$ is the general second law — essential for variable-mass (rocket) problems.
Momentum conservation holds in all collisions; kinetic energy only in elastic ones.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Momentum: $\vec{p} = m\vec{v}$ [kg·m/s]
Second law (general): $\vec{F} = \dfrac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$; constant mass: $\vec{F} = m\vec{a}$

Impulse–momentum theorem: $\vec{J} = \Delta\vec{p} = m\vec{v}_f - m\vec{v}_i$
Average force: $F_{avg} = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$

subtopics.name: Key points
points: Isolated system = no external force.
Momentum is always conserved in collisions.
Kinetic energy is conserved ONLY in elastic collisions.
Recoil and explosions are momentum conservation problems.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Conservation: $\sum \vec{p}_i = \sum \vec{p}_f$
1D Collision: $m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2$
Perfectly Inelastic: $m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = (m_1 + m_2) v$

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: Statement 1: Total momentum of an isolated system is constant.
Statement 2: Momentum is conserved in all collisions.

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: Exam Tip 1: Always state 'Assuming an isolated system' in theory answers.
Exam Tip 2: Check if the collision is elastic or inelastic before assuming KE conservation.
Trick 1: If objects stick, use $m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = (m_1 + m_2) v$.
Trick 2: Recoil: $V = -mv/M$.
Trick 3: Explosion: $m_1 v_1 = -m_2 v_2$.

subtopics.name: Key points
points: The FBD method is universal: isolate → draw forces → choose axes → ΣF = ma → solve.
The normal force adapts to the situation — it is NOT always mg.
Tension in an accelerating string differs from the weight of the attached mass.
Action-reaction pairs act on different bodies — never cancel in a single FBD.
On a frictionless incline, all bodies slide at the same rate (independent of mass).

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Newton's second law (vector): ΣF = ma → ΣF_x = ma_x, ΣF_y = ma_y
Elevator apparent weight: N = m(g ± a) where + is upward acceleration, − is downward
Atwood's machine: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂); T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂)
Smooth inclined plane: a = g sin θ down the slope; N = mg cos θ
Rough inclined plane: a = g(sin θ − μ cos θ); slides when tan θ > μ

subtopics.name: Key points
points: Torque = rF sin θ — it depends on force, distance, AND the angle between them.
Equilibrium requires BOTH ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0 — one without the other is not enough.
A couple produces pure rotation (zero net force, non-zero torque) — the torque is the same about any point.
The centre of gravity simplifies a distributed weight to a single point force.
Choose the pivot at an unknown force's point of application to eliminate that force from the torque equation.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Torque of a force: τ = rF sin θ (positive = anticlockwise, negative = clockwise)
Equilibrium conditions: ΣF = 0 (translational) AND Στ = 0 (rotational)
Couple torque: τ = F × d (independent of pivot position)
Centre of gravity: x_CG = Σ(mᵢxᵢ)/Σmᵢ (weighted average of positions)
Principle of moments: for equilibrium, sum of clockwise torques = sum of anticlockwise torques

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: Torque is the rotational effect of a force: τ = r × F (vector cross product), magnitude rF sin θ.
A rigid body is in static equilibrium if and only if ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0 about any point.

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: The FBD is essential — draw ALL forces with their correct points of application.
Choose the pivot wisely: at the point of an unknown force, that force contributes zero torque.
Ladder problems (smooth wall, rough ground) are standard — know the torque equation about the base.
Pivot trick: place the pivot at the point of an unknown force — that force drops out of the torque equation.
Seesaw shortcut: m₁r₁ = m₂r₂ — the product of mass and distance must be equal on both sides.

subtopics.name: Key points
points: Static friction is VARIABLE: it matches the applied force up to μ_sN.
Kinetic friction is approximately CONSTANT: f_k = μ_kN during sliding.
μ_k < μ_s — harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.
Friction is (approximately) independent of the apparent area of contact.
Pulling at an angle reduces N and friction; pushing at an angle increases both.

subtopics.name: Formulas & relations
points: Maximum static friction: f_s(max) = μ_sN (acts just before slipping)
Kinetic friction: f_k = μ_kN (acts during sliding; μ_k < μ_s)
Slope sliding condition: body slides when tan θ > μ_s; a = g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ)
Angle of friction: tan λ = μ_s (angle between normal and resultant reaction)
Angle of repose: tan θ_r = μ_s → θ_r = λ (steepest angle for rest)

subtopics.name: Statements to quote
points: Friction opposes relative motion (or its tendency) between two surfaces in contact.
Maximum static friction and kinetic friction are both proportional to the normal reaction: f_max = μN.
μ_k < μ_s for most surface pairs — it is harder to start sliding than to keep sliding.

subtopics.name: Exam focus
points: Slope problems are the most common — know the tan θ vs μ_s check and the a = g(sin θ − μ_k cos θ) formula.
Pulling/pushing at an angle changes the normal force — always recalculate N before finding friction.
Static friction is variable — do NOT assume f = μ_sN unless the body is at the point of slipping.
Slope check: compare tan θ with μ_s — if tan θ > μ_s, the body slides; otherwise it stays.
